section.title: Add It All Up
section.para: This program adds up the numbers from 1 to 10. sum collects the total, i walks from 1 upwards, and the loop goes on as long as i is at most 10. Beside the code you see how both of them grow, round after round.
section.programlisting: var sum 0 var i 1 while i <= 10 { sum := sum + i i := i + 1 } print "the sum is `sum`"
section.para: Your turn: change the program so that it adds up the numbers from 1 to 100. It should print the sum is 5050.
One number in the program says where the loop stops.
Change while i <= 10 to while i <= 100.
section.programlisting: var sum 0 var i 1 while i <= 100 { sum := sum + i i := i + 1 } print "the sum is `sum`"

section.title: Countdown
section.para: A loop can count downwards too: n starts at 3 and gets one smaller every round, until it reaches 0. Then the program prints one more line.
section.programlisting: var n 3 while n > 0 { print "`n`" n := n - 1 } print "Go!"
section.para: Your turn: make it count down from 10, and print Liftoff! at the end instead of Go!.
Two things change: where n starts, and the text of the last line.
var n 10 and print "Liftoff!".
section.programlisting: var n 10 while n > 0 { print "`n`" n := n - 1 } print "Liftoff!"

section.title: A Times Table
section.para: for i in 3 runs its body three times, with i being 0, 1 and 2. That is why the program writes i + 1: it wants to count from 1. Inside a text, backticks put the value of a calculation in.
Your turn: print the times table of 7, from 7 x 1 = 7 to 7 x 10 = 70.
How often must the loop run? And which number is multiplied?
for i in 10, and 7 in both places where the program says 3.

section.title: A Function of Your Own
section.para: A function takes values and gives one back. double takes a whole number n — an int — and returns an int: the last line of its body is what it gives back.
section.programlisting:
function double(n: int) returns int n * 2
print "double of 21 is `double(21)`"
section.para: Your turn: write a function square that multiplies a number by itself, and print square of 12 is 144 with it.
Copy the function double, call the copy square, and change what its body computes.
section.programlisting:
function square(n: int) returns int n * n
print "square of 12 is `square(12)`"

section.title: Even or Odd
section.para: % gives what is left over after dividing: 7 % 2 is 1, 8 % 2 is 0. A number is even when nothing is left over after dividing it by 2. if runs its line only when its condition holds.
Your turn: print only the even numbers from 1 to 6, each as 2 is even, 4 is even and so on.
An if before the print decides whether it runs. Comparing is written with a single =.
if n % 2 = 0, and below it, indented, print "`n` is even".
section.screen: 2 is even 4 is even 6 is even
